prompt: The same ten trades are put in a new order. What stays the same, and what can change?

options.text: The expectancy stays the same. The drawdown and the losing streaks can change.
Shuffling removes the edge, so the expectancy falls.
Everything changes, including the total result.
Only the win rate changes.

explanations.b: Shuffling does not change the trades or their total. The expectancy stays the same.
explanations.c: The total is the sum of the same trades, so it does not change with the order.
explanations.d: The win rate counts the wins, and the order does not change how many there are.

prompt: Hypothetical. A system has a loss probability of 0.65 on each trade. What is the chance, in percent, of three losses in a row starting at a given trade? Give the answer to one decimal place.
solution: 0.65 x 0.65 x 0.65 = 0.274625. As a percentage, that is 27.46 percent, which is about 27.5 percent to one decimal place.

prompt: A Monte Carlo run gives a 95th-percentile maximum drawdown of Rs 9,000. What does that mean?

options.text: Rs 9,000 is the worst drawdown that can happen.
In 95 runs out of every 100, the drawdown was Rs 9,000 or less.
The average drawdown is Rs 9,000.
The drawdown will be Rs 9,000 in 95 of the next 100 trades.

explanations.a: The 95th percentile is not the worst case. The worst run can be worse than it.
explanations.c: The average is a different figure. The 95th percentile is a point on the spread of results.
explanations.d: Simulated runs are not forecasts of your next trades.

prompt: Why is a shuffle-based run not fully realistic?

options.text: Shuffled results are realistic because they are random.
It assumes each trade is independent. Real losses often cluster, so the streaks can be understated.
It uses too many runs to be useful.
It cannot show results as percentages.

explanations.a: Random order is a tool for testing. It does not make each path a real path.
explanations.c: More runs help the spread of results. The run count is not the flaw.
explanations.d: Percentages are the usual way to read the results. They are not the limit.

prompt: Hypothetical. A Monte Carlo 95th-percentile drawdown is Rs 9,000. A friend says: 'So the rule will never lose more than Rs 9,000.' What is the best reply?

options.text: That is right, so the rule is safe at Rs 9,000.
No. The figure is a range from past trades under assumptions. It does not set a limit on future losses.
Yes, as long as the run used 1,000 shuffles.
No, because drawdown should only be given as a percentage.

explanations.a: A percentile is not a limit. Some runs were worse, and the future may differ from the past trades.
explanations.c: The number of shuffles does not turn a range into a promise. The assumptions still apply.
explanations.d: The unit is not the problem. The figure is a range, not a limit.

prompt: Statement: 'Monte Carlo shows the maximum drawdown I will suffer.' Which part of the statement is wrong?

options.text: The words 'Monte Carlo', because the method is a name for repeated random runs
The word 'shows', because Monte Carlo does not show any results
The words 'the maximum drawdown I will suffer', because they turn a range of simulated paths into a forecast of your future
Nothing. The statement is correct.

explanations.a: The name is fine. Monte Carlo is the name for the method of repeated random runs.
explanations.b: Monte Carlo does show results. Those results are a range of simulated paths, not nothing.
explanations.d: A simulation is not a forecast. The statement treats it as one, so it is wrong.
